summary: Defines requirements for emulating Time Division Multiplexed circuits, including PDH and SONET/SDH, across packet-switched networks. It is aligned with the Pseudo Wire Emulation Edge-to-Edge architecture. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4197 lists requirements for carrying TDM circuits over packet networks. It focuses on preserving the circuit's timing and handling packet loss, delay variation, signaling, and faults.

questions: tdm circuit emulation over packet networks
how do packet networks carry t1 and e1 circuits
subtitle: Requirements for carrying synchronous TDM circuits across packet-switched networks.

tldr.problem: Time Division Multiplexed (TDM) circuits carry data at fixed rates and depend on timing, while packet networks can vary packet arrival times and order.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds TDM-specific requirements to the PWE3 architecture for clock recovery, payload handling, packet loss and order, signaling, delay variation, congestion, and fault reporting.
tldr.outcome: It defines requirements for emulating PDH and SONET/SDH circuits over packet-switched networks; it does not specify an emulation protocol.

today: RFC 4197 is an Informational RFC published in October 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it specifies requirements rather than an emulation protocol.

sections.title: Why TDM Needs Specific Requirements
sections.content:
This RFC covers edge-to-edge emulation of circuits carrying Time Division Multiplexed (TDM) signals from the Plesiochronous Digital Hierarchy (PDH) and SONET/Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SDH). It follows the Pseudo Wire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) architecture and complements the general PWE3 requirements in RFC 3916.

TDM emulation needs to keep the clocks at the two ends in balance and keep the output clock's jitter and wander within applicable limits. Voice applications emphasize low one-way delay and tolerate some data errors; signaling applications can tolerate delay but are sensitive to errors.
sections.plainLanguage: TDM circuits depend on steady timing, while packet arrival times can vary. This RFC adds requirements for carrying TDM circuits over packet networks without losing the service's timing and behavior.

sections.title: TDM Structure and Transport Modes
sections.content:
Unstructured TDM is a raw bit stream with all bits available as payload. Structured TDM includes frames, channels called timeslots, and sometimes multiframes. The RFC gives T1 at 1.544 Mbps with 193-bit frames and E1 at 2.048 Mbps with 256-bit frames.

Structure-agnostic transport carries the stream and any structural overhead transparently. Structure-aware transport uses some of the structure; synchronization bits and related overhead may be removed at ingress and regenerated at egress. For channel signaling, the RFC describes Channel-Associated Signaling (CAS) and Common Channel Signaling (CCS).
sections.plainLanguage: A TDM stream may be carried as an undivided stream or as frames with identifiable channels. The transport can preserve all bits, or use some of the structure to process the circuit.

sections.title: Clock Recovery and Synchronization
sections.content:
The RFC's reference model identifies clocks at the customer and provider edges and across the network. The key requirement is that the recovered clock at one provider edge and the transmit clock at the other end have the same frequency.

It describes synchronized cases where the customer edges or provider edges share a reference clock, and relative or adaptive cases where timing must be recovered across the packet network. In the relative case, timing information MUST be transferred from the ingress provider edge to the egress provider edge. In the adaptive case, timing information MAY be transferred, for example using RTP.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends of an emulated circuit must transmit at matching clock rates. Depending on which clocks share a reference, timing may need to be carried across the packet network.

sections.title: Payload and Common Pseudowire Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC lists structure-agnostic services for E1, T1, E3, and T3. Structure-aware services include framed E1/T1, NxDS0 with or without CAS, and specified SONET/SDH circuits. It does not require structure-agnostic transport of SONET/SDH.

The encapsulation and payload layers must meet the relevant general PWE3 requirements. The encapsulation layer must provide sequencing and should provide timing information when required. It must provide connectivity between attachment circuits of the same type and sufficient synchronization to match the end-service clocks.
sections.plainLanguage: The document identifies which TDM services are in scope and what information their packets need. In particular, the emulation must preserve packet order and provide enough timing support for the circuit.

sections.title: Loss, Delay, Congestion, and Faults
sections.content:
The RFC allows an implementation to assume a very low packet-loss probability and does not require retransmission. The encapsulation should detect lost packets, limit their effect on clock recovery, and allow the egress to substitute appropriate data. Out-of-order packets must be detected and should be reordered when they are still suitable for playout; otherwise they are treated as lost.

Packetization and compensation buffers affect bandwidth and delay. Because TDM circuits have a constant rate, TCP-style rate adjustment does not apply. The ability to shut down a TDM pseudowire when congestion is detected MUST be provided. The encapsulation should also detect and report misconnection, packet loss, and malformed packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Lost packets are not retransmitted, so the receiver needs to detect gaps and keep the circuit clock stable. The network must also provide a way to shut down a circuit when congestion is detected.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations in RFC 3916 apply to TDM emulation. RFC 4197 adds that TDM services are sensitive to packet delay variation and need protection from attacks that exploit it.
sections.plainLanguage: Uneven packet delays can affect TDM service. The RFC says the service needs protection from attacks that cause such variation.
